 OPINION: Passion shouldn't come with a price
 New federal student loan limits raise concerns about how the government values degrees that don't guarantee high-paying careers
 By Ella Finkelstein 
 November 6, 2026 | 9:00am EST 
 A new bill by the Trump Administration regards certain degrees professionalism may have adverse effects on smaller fields such as the arts. Despite these smaller fields being less popular than STEM related fields they still hold value.
 Photo by Anenaa Kumar |
 The Independent Florida Alligator
 Most teenagers look forward to breaking high school’s mundane and repetitive routine in college, experimenting with unfamiliar subjects, discovering their passions and finding out who they want to become. 
 However, taking advantage of these opportunities to experiment with different programs and classes is becoming increasingly difficult. 
 On July 24, 2025 , President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law. Some changes went into effect right away, while others didn't until July 1, 2026.  The bill limits the amount of federal student loans offered, aiming to hold colleges accountable for programs and majors that leave students with low financial outcomes after graduation. Majors that fail to meet these earnings will be at risk of losing access to federal student loans and Pell Grants . Consequently, high earning STEM majors are treated with more merit than majors not projected to return on these loans, which include the humanities and arts. 
 Many students are forced to take on loans just to attend a university. We should discourage students from taking on an immense amount of debt that will be difficult to pay off — it’s not a good way to start off  adulthood. It is upsetting to admit that financial outcomes do matter, and if a degree is not projected to be profitable, it could be wise to choose something else. 
 Although, what does it say about the education system if only certain majors are suffering from the cutbacks?  
 The humanities and arts are currently viewed as less valuable than science and mathematics majors. In truth, the humanities and arts are the framework for society.
 The humanities allow us to contextualize the world, understanding people’s beliefs, religions and culture. It is essential to learn what makes us human as it aids in relating and communicating with our peers. That knowledge becomes increasingly important as technology and artificial intelligence dehumanize society. Critical thinking and thoughtful analyses are becoming rare skills that must be preserved. 
 The arts are also essential; they can provoke society to reflect and question our own ideas instead of accepting concepts at face value. The arts also drive human connection and creativity. Without creativity, there would be no innovation. 
 Just because a humanities degree may not be as profitable as a doctor or engineer, it doesn’t mean passionate students should not pursue them. They are crucial to society. 
 Since when have we decided that education should prepare students to make a salary rather than make a difference? 
 Going through education with the only goal of making a profit isn’t a beneficial mindset. Education is about equipping students with the skills and knowledge to foster their talents and lead a fulfilling life. We should be focusing on how we can positively contribute to society. If no one focuses on finding their purpose and making a difference, then what is the point of an education? We are worth more than a paycheck. 
 Financial outcomes matter, but they shouldn't be the only measure of an education's worth.
